sofar.title: Chunk 2: a reroute does measurable damage, and it is small on an idle path
sofar.summary: A single 10 Mbit/s TCP flow was moved between spines once, with one OFPFC_MODIFY_STRICT on the ingress leaf, and watched for 2 s after the flow-mod’s barrier reply. Every slow-to-fast move produced reordering and spurious retransmissions; no control did. The goodput lost in those 2 s was 0.29% at a 4 ms delay gap and 2.81% at a 9 ms gap. The cause is the one the proposal predicted: packets on the new, faster path overtake packets still on the old one, the sender retransmits segments that were never lost, and cwnd is cut. In all 80 trials the kernel never undid that cut. With one flow on an idle path the cut costs almost nothing, which is the caveat. Chunk 3 tests the same mechanism with competing flows.

columns: Goodput deficit in 2 s vs control
rows: no reroute (controls on 1, 5 and 10 ms spines)

notes: Retransmissions after a move are almost all spurious: the retransmitted-segment count matches the DSACK count in every reroute condition (R1 5.2 vs 5.0, R2 8.6 vs 6.3, R0 5.2 vs 5.2, R3 3.0 vs 3.0 per move).
R2’s deficit is dominated by 3 of 10 trials that hit a retransmission timeout; the other 7 lose 10.8 KB each (post-hoc table in verdict.md, not part of the verdict).
Steady goodput before every move was 9.564 Mbit/s of 10. Flow-mod to barrier reply took a median of 1.15 ms, so the move itself drops nothing; the damage is TCP behaviour.
A second run of R2 and C1 as root on the system Open vSwitch agreed with the rootless campaign.
